title: Titanic, 3,800 m Down
blurb: She sank in 1912 and was not found until 1985, lying in two pieces under 380 atmospheres in permanent darkness at about 1 °C. Iron-eating bacteria are taking her apart from the inside; the rust hangs off the hull in icicles that had no name until she was found.

title: Every Drop Has Been Everywhere
sub: The planet has had the same water for four billion years
blurb: Water leaves the ocean as vapour, falls as rain, runs down rivers and returns. Almost none is created and almost none is lost, so the water in your glass has been through clouds, rivers, animals and the deep sea more times than can be counted.

title: The Moon Lifts the Ocean
sub: Two bulges, and two high tides a day
blurb: The Moon pulls the near side of the ocean toward it and pulls the Earth away from the far side, leaving a bulge at both ends. The coast then rotates through them. In the Bay of Fundy the difference between high and low water reaches 16 metres.
stats: one bulge pulled, one left behind

title: The River That Out-Pours Seven
sub: A fifth of all the river water on Earth
blurb: The Amazon discharges around 209,000 cubic metres a second — more than the next seven largest rivers combined. Its plume of fresh, silted water stays recognisable hundreds of kilometres out to sea, and ships once refilled their barrels out of sight of land.
stats: Share of river water reaching the sea

title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch
blurb: A gyre of currents concentrates floating plastic across roughly 1.6 million square kilometres. You could sail through it and see almost nothing: most of it is fragments smaller than a grain of rice, suspended through the water rather than floating on it — which is exactly why it is so hard to clean up.

title: The Global Conveyor
sub: One lap takes a thousand years
blurb: Warm surface water flows north, cools, grows salty and sinks, then crawls back along the sea floor for centuries before welling up again on the other side of the world. Water sinking off Greenland today will surface in the Pacific in roughly a thousand years.
stats: it is why Europe is mild
